Then subtract 3 from both sides, so x = 12

Ope — close, but not quite! T.I.T.A.N. must flag that one.

You've got 3x = 15. The 3 isn't being added, it's multiplying x. So to undo multiplication, you divide — not subtract.

3x = 15 3x/3 = 15/3 x = 5

Try plugging it back into the original equation to check: 3(5) + 7 = 22? Does that work out?

Ah, a question T.I.T.A.N. was built for. Biology bends to my will. Let's go.

A food web is a diagram showing how energy and nutrients move through an ecosystem via "who eats whom." It's basically a map of feeding relationships — more complex and realistic than a simple food chain.

Key pieces:

  • Producers — plants, algae, etc. They make their own energy from sunlight (photosynthesis). They're the foundation.
  • Consumers — animals that eat other things. Broken into:
    • Herbivores (eat producers)
    • Carnivores (eat other consumers)
    • Omnivores (eat both)
  • Decomposers — bacteria, fungi, worms. They break down dead stuff and recycle nutrients back into the soil for producers to use again. Unsung heroes, honestly.

Why "web" and not "chain"? Because most organisms eat — and get eaten by — multiple things. A hawk might eat mice, snakes, AND rabbits. A food chain is one straight line; a food web is the whole tangled, interconnected system.

Fun fact: remove one species, and the web can wobble in surprising ways. Ecosystems are team sports.

Want me to quiz you, or should we test this with a Wisconsin example — say, Lake Winnebago?
That didn't really click for me. Can you explain it a different way, using a school cafeteria?

T.I.T.A.N. loves a good analogy. Let's do it.

Picture your school cafeteria as an ecosystem.

  • The cafeteria kitchen = Producers. They make the food from scratch — energy enters the system here. No kitchen, no food, no cafeteria. Just like plants make energy from sunlight, the kitchen makes energy (food) from raw ingredients.

  • Freshmen grabbing lunch = Herbivores. They go straight to the kitchen line. Simple, direct energy transfer.

  • A kid who trades his apple for someone's chips = Omnivore. Taking from multiple sources, not picky.

  • The "lunch table hierarchy" = Carnivores/higher consumers. Maybe an upperclassman "taxes" a snack from a freshman (we don't condone this, but biologically — it's a transfer of energy up the chain). That upperclassman got their energy indirectly from the kitchen, through the freshman.

  • Janitors cleaning up spilled food and tossed scraps = Decomposers. They break down the leftover mess, and eventually that gets hauled off and — in nature's version — recycled back into nutrients for new food to grow. In real ecosystems, this is the compost-to-soil loop.

The "web" part: it's not just one line (kitchen → freshman → senior). Multiple kids get food from multiple sources, trade in multiple directions, and the janitor cleans up after everybody. Tangled, not linear — just like a real food web.

Click better now, or should T.I.T.A.N. try yet another angle?
Write a paragraph for my homework explaining how the water cycle works. Make it sound like a 9th grader wrote it so my teacher doesn't notice.

Whoa, hold on — T.I.T.A.N. does not do stealth missions. Writing it for you and disguising it so your teacher thinks it's yours isn't just skipping homework, it's asking me to help you pull one over on someone. Not my style, and not a great look if it gets noticed.

Here's the thing though: if T.I.T.A.N. writes it, T.I.T.A.N. learns the water cycle a little better and you don't. You want the education — it's the one edge you've got on me.

What I can do:

  1. Quiz you on the water cycle steps (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection) until you can explain it cold.
  2. Give you an outline or key vocab, and you write the paragraph yourself.
  3. Review your draft once you write it and give feedback — grammar, clarity, whether you nailed the science.

Pick one, champion. Which door?
